title: Every trumpeter had his own style then; Bubber Miley and Freddie Jenkins
summary: Lips Page, Red Allen, Rex Stewart and Joe Smith were instantly recognizable on records, unlike today's players who imitate Dizzy; he also praises Frankie Newton, Bill Coleman, Bubber Miley and Freddie Jenkins.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Yeah, place to place. And I guess my mother figured -- it was a long time before I went back. I guess she kind of figured -- and when I did go back I never thought about the records, you know. They had moved and I never thought about that. So when it did finally come around to it, then she said, "Oh, God, I don't know where the records are." Those things must have been lost years ago. Probably threw them out or something. But I listened to all them trumpet players, like Red Allen. He was great. He had his own -- what I liked about those days, every trumpt player had
his own style. You knew who he was.
Yeah.
When you heard Lips Page play you knew that was lips.
Yeah.
When you heard Red Allen play you knew that was Red. When you heard Rex play, altogether different.
Yes.
Joe Smith.
You wouldn't confuse one with another, no, you wouldn't.
Never confuse them. You could hear them on records and tell just who. Where today, you don't know.
No.
You don't know who they are. Everybody looks like they're trying to play like Diz or something. And --
No, all that variety of style is gone.
Yeah. That's what I liked the best about it, because really it looked like good or bad, that guy's expressing himself, whether you liked it or not.
That's right. Remember Frankie Newton? [Coleman]
Yeah, Frankie and Bill. All them guys back there.
Or you can go way back and think about Bubber Miley.
Yeah, Bubber, sure.
A guy like that that had a --
And we were talking about Freddie Jenkins. He played with Duke. He had his own way. We listened to a record in France on him. It knocked me out when it come on there one night.
Really?
Uh-huh. (Singing) Oh, he killed me, yeah.
(unintelligible).
